title: Virtual Morris Water Task for Spatial Navigation and Memory Assessment
author: Thornberry, Cimadevilla, et al.
materials: It is particularly important to control for non‐learning effects (such as movement, visual, and motivation) during task acquisition, especially when trying to correlate neural markers (e.g., fMRI, EEG, and MEG) to learning and memory performance; these are seldom included within the experimental design. As previously discussed in Thornberry et al. (2021) and Vorhees & Williams (2006), common control procedures for the MWM task include allowing animals to swim freely around the pool for the same period as the learning counterparts (Shires & Aggleton, 2008). Others used cued or beacon learning groups, but this “control” still involves a form of learning (Barry & Commins, 2019; Wolbers & Wiener, 2014). VWM approaches have been similar, using free movement conditions for the same length of time as learning trials or cued learning (Goodrich‐Hunsaker et al., 2010). Similarly, in a recent study that analyzed EEG correlates during spatial learning and recall, Thornberry & Commins (2024) used a separate non‐learning group that was required to explore the same environment as a learning group but without a target being present. Each trial in the non‐learning group was time‐matched to the mean time taken by the learning group to reach the target. Furthermore, any control group should be matched for age, gender, and other demographics.

steps.title: Prepare participant and equipment
steps.instruction: Set up the participant in the experimental space (VR or neural recording system) or place them in a distraction‑free room in front of a computer (desktop).

steps.title: Display environment and start position
steps.instruction: Show the virtual arena from a first‑person view, position the participant at one of the four cardinal points, and present any on‑screen or verbal instructions.

steps.title: Run navigation trial and record data
steps.instruction: Allow the participant to navigate using the chosen controller (joystick, keyboard, mouse). Start timing when movement begins; stop timing when the hidden target is reached or when the trial time elapses (minimum recommended duration 1 min). Record the latency and, if possible, the path length via the software.

substeps.instruction: Start timer when participant begins moving
Stop timer when target reached or trial time (≥1 min) expires
Record latency and, if possible, path length using the software

steps.title: Guide participant if target missed
steps.instruction: If the participant does not locate the hidden goal within the trial time limit, manually guide them to the goal location.

steps.title: Implement inter‑trial interval and repeat
steps.instruction: Provide an inter‑trial interval (ITI) of at least 5 % of the total trial time (e.g., 3 s for a 60‑s trial) before starting the next trial at a new start location. Continue repeating steps 2–4 until the predetermined number of trials is completed (e.g., 12 trials). Adjust ITI length only if the environment is unusually easy (shorter) or extremely challenging (longer).

substeps.instruction: Calculate ITI as ≥5 % of trial duration
Ensure ITI meets minimum (e.g., 3 s for 60 s trial)
Start next trial at a new start location
Repeat until preset trial count reached

steps.title: Record target time during ITI
steps.instruction: During each ITI, record the time the participant spends on the target and report this metric in subsequent analyses, especially for trials where the platform was not found within the trial time.
